newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura's Yoshihisa Tabuchi says never met Koike.
newsitem.headline: Nomura's Yoshihisa Tabuchi says never met Koike.

text.p: A former president of Nomura Securities Co Ltd, Yoshihisa Tabuchi, said on Thursday he had never met corporate racketeer Ryuichi Koike, the man at the centre of a payoff scandal involving Nomura.
"I have never met Koike," Tabuchi told a committee of the Lower House of parliament.
Tabuchi was summoned to speak before the budget committee as an unsworn witness regarding the Nomura scandal.

Hideo Sakamaki, who took over the presidency from Tabuchi when Tabuchi stepped down in 1991, was arrested last week on suspicion of conspiring with three Nomura executives to pay 38.5 million yen in 1995 to Koike.
Koike and his younger brother were arrested last month on suspicion of taking 50 million yen in payments from Nomura after threatening to disrupt the company's 1995 annual shareholders meeting.
At the 1995 annual meeting, Tabuchi and former Nomura chairman Setsuya Tabuchi were approved as directors. The two men are not related.

Public criticism over the appointment of the two Tabuchis was strong at that time, as they had resigned their positions in 1991 over a scandal in which, according to Japanese media, Nomura had compensated elite clients for losses and its affiliates had contacts with gangsters.

Tabuchi, now an adviser to Nomura, said he told current Nomura president Junichi Ujiie last week that he intended to resign as an adviser. "I said I would resign," he told the committee. He said he had been asked by Sakamaki to return as a director to help Nomura in Asian business in 1995, but said he was not involved in any wrongdoing.
"I was asked (to do so). I don't know how things happened after that," he said.
Asked if Sakamaki talked to him about Sakamaki's meeting with racketeer Koike in 1992, Tabuchi said he had not kown that Sakamaki had met Koike.
On Wednesay last week, Sakamaki told another parliamentary committee that he met Koike on one occasion in 1992 after becoming president.

Asked whether he had met other racketeers, Tabuchi said he has not met any people known as "sokaiya", but said he was acquainted with the late Rikiya Kijima, a former publishing company president who Japanese media reports have said was a noted racketeer.
Tabuchi said he met Kijima more than 10 years ago as a publisher, but said he did not know he was a racketeer until recently.

Kijima, said to have been a mentor to Ryuichi Koike, has been reported by Japanese media to have been close to the late Yoshio Kodama, a political "fixer" with gangster and right-wing links who was a key figure in the early 1970s Lockheed payoff scandal that involved former prime minister Kakuei Tanaka.

Tabuchi denied that Nomura gave some politicians and bureaucrats preferential treatment in return for their help in making a success of an industrial park development project in Vietnam. The project, led by Nomura, started in 1994 and was completed in 1997.
Nomura did not try to involve Japanese politicians and bureaucrats in the project, he told the committee.

Japanese media reports have said Nomura operated "VIP accounts" offering preferential treatment to selected customers. Nomura denied the existence of such special accounts and argued the term was not intended to mean "Very Important Persons".
Nomura said recently it had started using the term "VIP" as a label for certain customers from 1983, when it computerised a system for supervising client information.

Accounts were labelled "VIP" if the clients needed careful treatment such as when sending them mail about transactions, the firm said, adding that it had stopped using the term from April to avoid any further "misunderstanding" about its usage.
Politicians, senior bureaucrats and business leaders were among those said to be holding VIP accounts at Nomura, Japan's largest brokerage firm, according to media reports.
Tokyo prosecutors are said to be looking closely into whether there was more to being a VIP account holder.
On Wednesday, prosecutors said Nomura itself had been indicted for violation of securities law by illegally compensating for trading losses a firm owned by the brother of a racketeer.
Two former Nomura directors have been indicted for allegedly giving 49.7 million yen to racketeer Ryoichi Koike in March 1995 in violation of Japan's Securities and Exchange Law and Commercial Code.
